title: The Sabbath, part 1: the biblical Sabbath

series.title: The Sabbath: God's day of rest
series.share: Three studies: the biblical Sabbath, what Jesus said about it, and Romans 14, the seasons and life today.

share: How much does the Sabbath matter to the Father? From creation to the prophets: no work, a sign, and a delight.
opening_question: God rested on the seventh day, blessed it and made it holy. How important is the Sabbath to the Father? What does "no work" mean in the Law, how seriously did He take it, when does the day begin and end, and why do the prophets call it both a warning and a delight? This is part 1 of 3. Each step asks what the text says and what it means for me.

steps.intro: Background first: God made all things in six days, and each day closed with "the evening and the morning" (Genesis 1:5).
steps.question: What did God do on the seventh day, and what three things does Genesis 2 say He did with it?
steps.apply: Do I treat rest as a gift from God, or as something I have to earn?

facts.text: "rested" is shabath, Strong's: "to repose that is desist from exertion". The word sabbath, shabbath, comes from it: "intermission".
God did not rest because He was tired: He "fainteth not, neither is weary". He rested because the work was "finished".
God "blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it". "sanctified" is qadash; Strong's lists "consecrate", "hallow" and "sanctify". It is the first time the Bible uses this word.
Genesis does not use the word sabbath here, and it records no command to Adam. Readers differ on whether the day was kept from creation or first given to Israel.

steps.question: Before Sinai, what did the LORD give Israel on the sixth day, what were they to do with it, and what happened when some went out to gather on the seventh day?
steps.apply: Do I trust God enough to stop, even when there seems to be more to gather?

facts.text: This is the first time the Bible uses the word sabbath: "To morrow is the rest of the holy sabbath unto the LORD".
The rest was prepared for: "on the sixth day they shall prepare that which they bring in", "bake that which ye will bake to day".
Manna kept overnight on other days "bred worms, and stank". The portion kept for the sabbath "did not stink, neither was there any worm therein".
The LORD asked: "How long refuse ye to keep my commandments and my laws?" And He called it a gift: "the LORD hath given you the sabbath".

steps.question: How do the two tellings of the fourth commandment begin, who must rest, and what reason does each one give?
steps.apply: Who in my home or at my work depends on me to give them rest?

facts.text: Exodus begins "Remember the sabbath day"; Deuteronomy begins "Keep the sabbath day". It is the only one of the Ten Commandments that begins with "Remember".
Exodus gives creation as the reason: "in six days the LORD made heaven and earth". Deuteronomy gives the exodus: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt".
The rest reached everyone: children, servants, cattle and "thy stranger that is within thy gates", "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou".
"rested" in Exodus 20:11 is nuach, Strong's: "to rest that is settle down". Exodus 23 adds that the ox, the servant and the stranger "may be refreshed".

steps.intro: No work: what the Law says, even in the busiest season of the year.
steps.question: What does the Law say about work on the seventh day, even "in earing time and in harvest"? What else was not to be done in their habitations?
steps.apply: What do I call too important to stop for, and what does that say about what I trust?

facts.text: "in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest". Earing is ploughing. The two busiest times of a farmer's year were no exception.
"ye shall do no work therein: it is the sabbath of the LORD in all your dwellings". The day was kept at home, not only at the tabernacle.
"Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day". Readers differ on whether this meant all fire or the fire of work, such as cooking and the forge.
It is "an holy day, a sabbath of rest to the LORD". The day belongs to the LORD; man's ordinary work stops.

steps.intro: How seriously the Father took it: one case in the wilderness.
steps.question: What did the man in the wilderness do on the sabbath day, why was he put in ward, and what did the LORD say should be done?
steps.apply: Do I take lightly what God takes seriously?

facts.text: He "gathered sticks upon the sabbath day". They put him in ward "because it was not declared what should be done to him": Moses waited for the LORD.
The law had already said: "whosoever doeth any work therein, that soul shall be cut off from among his people", and "he shall surely be put to death".
This case comes right after the law for sins done "presumptuously", the one who "hath despised the word of the LORD". Many read the stick-gatherer as an example of that open defiance.

Under the law of Moses this was carried out by the whole congregation, "as the LORD commanded Moses". Christians differ on how the penalties of the law of Moses apply after the cross; the seriousness of the day is not in doubt.

steps.question: What does God call the sabbath in Exodus 31 and Ezekiel 20, between whom, for how long, and what does it show about who sanctifies His people?
steps.apply: What does the shape of my week show about whom I belong to?

facts.text: "sign" is 'owth, Strong's: "a signal", "as a flag". It is "a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever".
The sign is "that ye may know that I am the LORD that doth sanctify you". Ezekiel repeats it, and adds "hallow my sabbaths".
God speaks of "my sabbaths". Ezekiel lists among Israel's sins in the wilderness: "my sabbaths they greatly polluted".
"and was refreshed" is naphash, Strong's: "to breathe", "to be breathed upon". God's rest is pictured as taking a breath.
It is called "a perpetual covenant". Some read this as binding on all God's people for ever; others read it as the sign of the covenant made with Israel at Sinai.

steps.intro: Background first: in the Bible a day begins at evening. "the evening and the morning were the first day" (Genesis 1:5).
steps.question: When does a Bible day begin and end? What did Nehemiah do "when the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the sabbath"?
steps.apply: How could I prepare before a day of rest begins, so that it is truly rest?

facts.text: The Day of Atonement, a yearly sabbath, was kept "from even unto even". "even" is ereb, Strong's: "dusk".
Nehemiah shut the gates as dusk came "before the sabbath" and kept them shut "till after the sabbath".
Jews have kept the weekly sabbath the same way, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset. Part 2 shows the Gospels counting it the same way.

steps.question: What did Jeremiah promise if Judah would "hallow the sabbath day", what did he warn if they would not, and what did Nehemiah find and do?
steps.apply: Where do buying, selling and busyness crowd out my rest with God?

facts.text: The promise: "this city shall remain for ever". The warning: "then will I kindle a fire in the gates thereof".
Nehemiah asked the nobles: "What evil thing is this that ye do, and profane the sabbath day?" and reminded them: "Did not your fathers thus".
Amos shows the heart behind it: "When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat".
Nehemiah set guards at the gates "to sanctify the sabbath day", and prayed "Remember me, O my God, concerning this also".

steps.intro: Closing: the prophets do not only warn. They call the day a delight and open it to all who come.
steps.question: What does Isaiah call the sabbath, what does God promise the stranger and the eunuch who keep it, and what will all flesh do "from one sabbath to another"?
steps.apply: Is my day of rest a burden I carry, or a delight I look forward to?

facts.text: "call the sabbath a delight": "delight" is oneg, Strong's: "luxury".
Isaiah ties the day to the heart: "not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words". The promise: "Then shalt thou delight thyself in the LORD".
Isaiah 56 opens the sabbath to outsiders: "the sons of the stranger" who keep it, "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people". Jesus quoted this in the temple.
In the new heavens and the new earth, "from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me". Readers differ on whether this is the weekly day or a picture of unbroken worship.

remember.text: "God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it"
"Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy"
"in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest"
"that ye may know that I am the LORD that doth sanctify you"
"from even unto even, shall ye celebrate your sabbath"
"call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable"
